title: Media & Visual Literacy
description: Analyse advertisements, posters, film shots and visual texts. Learn how images, layout, colour, typography and camera choices create meaning and influence audiences.

notes.heading: What is Visual Literacy?
notes.body: Visual literacy is the ability to read, understand and critically analyse visual texts — images, advertisements, posters, films, memes, infographics and more. Just like written texts, visual texts communicate meaning through deliberate choices. In MYP, you analyse how visual elements (colour, layout, typography, images, symbols) work together to create messages, moods and responses. A 'text' is not only words; any piece of communication that can be interpreted is a text. Being visually literate means asking: Who created this? What is the purpose? Who is the audience? What techniques are used, and what effect do they have?

illustration.alt: A sample advertisement poster labelled with visual literacy techniques including colour, image, slogan, typography, layout and target audience.
illustration.caption: Advertisements combine visual elements to persuade viewers. Each choice is deliberate and carries meaning.

notes.heading: Analysing Advertisements
notes.body: Advertisements are designed to persuade viewers to think, feel or do something. They combine images, words, logos and design. Start with the big picture: what product, service or idea is being promoted? Then examine the techniques. The slogan is a short, memorable phrase that captures the message. The image often shows an idealised lifestyle or emotion associated with the product. A logo builds brand recognition. Celebrity or expert endorsement adds credibility (ethos). Fine print, disclaimers and prices may be hidden in small text. Ask: what need, fear or desire does the ad appeal to? How does it try to make the viewer feel?

notes.heading: Visual Techniques in Posters
notes.body: Posters use a compact combination of visual techniques to attract attention and communicate quickly. Colour sets mood: red can suggest passion, urgency or danger; blue often suggests calm, trust or technology; green suggests nature, health or growth. Contrast draws the eye to key areas. Size and scale show importance — larger elements are usually more significant. Rule of thirds places the main subject off-centre to create visual interest. Balance can be symmetrical (formal, stable) or asymmetrical (dynamic, energetic). Typography includes font choice, size, weight and spacing. A bold sans-serif font may feel modern and strong; a script font may feel elegant or personal.

notes.heading: Symbols and Visual Codes
notes.body: Symbols are objects, colours or images that stand for larger ideas. A dove symbolises peace; a red cross symbolises medical help; a crown symbolises power or royalty. Visual codes are repeated conventions that audiences learn to recognise. In film and advertising, lighting codes matter: bright, high-key lighting often suggests happiness or innocence; dark, low-key lighting suggests mystery or danger. Costumes, settings and props also carry coded meanings. A character in a suit may be coded as professional or powerful; a natural setting may code a product as wholesome or eco-friendly. Effective visual analysis explains both what the symbol is and what it means in context.

notes.heading: Reading Film Shots
notes.body: Film shots are visual texts created through camera choices. Shot size controls what we see and how we feel: extreme close-up (intense emotion, detail), close-up (facial expression, personal connection), medium shot (character and some context), long shot (setting, isolation or scale). Camera angle matters: low angle makes a subject look powerful or threatening; high angle makes them look weak or vulnerable; eye-level is neutral and relatable. Movement creates energy: a tracking shot follows action; a static shot can feel calm or observational. Lighting, colour grading and framing all add meaning. When analysing a film shot, connect technique to effect: 'The low-angle close-up makes the character appear dominant and intimidating.'

notes.heading: Purpose, Audience and Context
notes.body: Every visual text is created for a reason and for a specific audience. Purpose: to inform, persuade, entertain, sell, raise awareness or provoke. Audience: who is meant to see it? Consider age, gender, interests, values, language and cultural background. Context: when, where and how was it made and shared? A poster from the 1950s reflects different social values from a poster today. A social media ad is designed for fast scrolling, so it uses bold images and minimal text. A government health campaign may use clear, trustworthy design. Always link technique to purpose and audience: 'The bright colours and cartoon characters appeal to young children, while the simple safety message reassures parents.'

notes.heading: Writing a Visual Analysis
notes.body: A strong visual analysis follows a clear structure. Introduction: identify the visual text, creator, context and overall purpose. Body paragraphs: each focuses on one technique or element. Use the TEEL structure: Technique (name the visual choice), Example (describe it precisely), Effect (explain the impact on the viewer), Link (connect back to purpose or audience). Use specific vocabulary: foreground, background, focal point, gaze, composition, contrast, saturation, framing, vector, salience. Avoid simply listing what you see; analyse how it creates meaning. Conclusion: summarise the overall message and evaluate how effectively the visual text achieves its purpose. Remember to discuss the interaction of visuals and any words present.

flashcards.definition: The ability to read, understand and critically analyse visual texts such as images, ads, posters and film shots.
flashcards.example: Interpreting how colour and layout in an advertisement create a feeling of luxury.

flashcards.definition: A short, memorable phrase used in advertisements to capture the main message or idea.
flashcards.example: 'Just Do It' — Nike's famous slogan encourages action and determination.

flashcards.definition: A visual symbol or design that identifies a brand, company or organisation.
flashcards.example: The golden arches immediately identify McDonald's.

flashcards.definition: A composition technique where the image is divided into a 3x3 grid and key elements are placed along the lines or intersections.
flashcards.example: A poster places the main character at the left intersection to create visual interest.

flashcards.definition: A camera angle looking up at a subject, often making it appear powerful, heroic or intimidating.
flashcards.example: A film shows the villain from below to make them seem dominant.

flashcards.definition: A camera angle looking down at a subject, often making it appear weak, vulnerable or insignificant.
flashcards.example: A character lost in a crowd is filmed from above to suggest isolation.

flashcards.definition: An object, colour or image that represents a larger idea or meaning.
flashcards.example: A dove symbolises peace; a red rose symbolises love.

flashcards.definition: The degree to which an element stands out and attracts the viewer's attention.
flashcards.example: A bright red button on a grey website has high salience.

flashcards.definition: The difference between light and dark, colours or sizes used to draw attention and create visual interest.
flashcards.example: Black text on a white background creates strong contrast and readability.

flashcards.definition: A line or direction within an image that guides the viewer's eye through the composition.
flashcards.example: A road leading into the distance points the viewer's gaze toward the horizon.

flashcards.definition: The direction a person in an image is looking; can direct the viewer's attention or create a relationship with the audience.
flashcards.example: A model looking directly at the viewer creates a personal, engaging address.

flashcards.definition: The use of colour to represent ideas or emotions, such as red for passion or danger, blue for calm or trust.
flashcards.example: An environmental poster uses green to suggest nature and sustainability.

choices: The ability to draw realistic pictures
The ability to read, understand and analyse visual texts
The ability to use a camera
questions.explanation: Visual literacy means being able to interpret and critically analyse visual texts such as advertisements, posters, film shots and images, not just create them.

questions.stem: In a poster, a large image placed off-centre using the rule of thirds is most likely intended to:
choices: Make the poster easier to print
Create visual interest and direct the viewer's eye
questions.explanation: The rule of thirds places key elements along grid lines or intersections to create balance, interest and a natural viewing path.

questions.stem: A low-angle shot of a character usually suggests:
choices: The character is weak and frightened
The character is powerful or intimidating
questions.explanation: Low-angle shots look up at the subject, which typically makes the subject appear dominant, powerful or threatening.

questions.stem: Which colour is most commonly associated with calm, trust and technology in advertisements?
questions.explanation: Blue is widely used to suggest calmness, reliability, professionalism and technology.

questions.stem: A short, memorable phrase such as 'Just Do It' in an advertisement is called a:
questions.explanation: A slogan is a brief, catchy phrase that captures the main message or attitude of an advertisement or brand.

questions.stem: A government health poster uses clear fonts, simple icons and neutral colours. Its purpose is most likely to:
questions.explanation: Clear, simple and neutral design choices suggest the purpose is to inform the public clearly and build trust.

questions.stem: A red cross on a white background is an example of:
choices: A logo for a sports brand
questions.explanation: A red cross is a widely recognised symbol for medical aid, health services and humanitarian organisations.

questions.stem: In a film, an extreme close-up of a character's eyes is most likely used to:
choices: Create intense emotion or reveal detail
questions.explanation: Extreme close-ups isolate small details and intensify emotion, drawing the audience into the character's inner state.

questions.stem: Which term describes the path or direction that guides the viewer's eye through an image?
questions.explanation: A vector is a visual line or direction in an image that leads the viewer's gaze from one point to another.

questions.stem: A poster uses bright colours, cartoon characters and playful fonts. Who is the likely target audience?
questions.explanation: Bright colours, cartoon characters and playful typography are visual codes commonly aimed at young children.

questions.stem: What does 'high-key lighting' in a film scene usually suggest?
choices: Happiness, innocence or an upbeat mood
questions.explanation: High-key lighting is bright and even with few shadows, often used to create cheerful, safe or innocent atmospheres.

questions.stem: A brand symbol such as the golden arches of McDonald's is best described as a:
questions.explanation: A logo is a distinctive visual design or symbol that identifies a company, product or organisation.

questions.stem: When a person in an advertisement looks directly at the viewer, this technique is called:
questions.explanation: Gaze refers to where a person in an image is looking; direct gaze can create a personal connection with the audience.

questions.stem: A film director films a lost character from high above a crowded street. The effect is to suggest:
choices: The character is isolated or vulnerable
questions.explanation: High-angle shots look down on a subject and can make characters appear small, vulnerable or overwhelmed by their surroundings.

questions.stem: In visual analysis, the TEEL paragraph structure helps you:
choices: List all the colours in an image
Organise technique, example, effect and link to purpose
Count the number of words in a slogan
Decide whether you like the image
questions.explanation: TEEL stands for Technique, Example, Effect, Link. It structures analysis by connecting visual choices to their impact and the text's purpose.
